newsitem.title: USA: TWA pays San Francisco fees bringing carrier current.
newsitem.headline: TWA pays San Francisco fees bringing carrier current.

text.p: Trans World Airlines Inc., which had owed the San Francisco International Airport nearly $1 million in fees, has made a $650,000 payment to bring the carrier current, an airport spokesman said.
Not all of the fees were due immediately.
"TWA wired us a check for full payment up to and including April 1," said Ron Wilson, a spokesman for the San Francisco International airport.
Earlier, he had said TWA would be notified next week that its lease would be terminated unless payment was received.
He said St. Louis-based TWA owed about $980,000 for landing fees and space rental, and had not made a payment to San Franciso airport since early February.

TWA, whose independent auditors have raised concerns about its ability to remain a going company, declined to comment specifically on fees it owes to San Franciso or other airports. A spokesman, however, said the airline has not been served any eviction or termination notices.
"We have not at any time been served or sent an eviction notice for San Francisco, or by Dallas/Fort Worth or any airport," Donn Walker, a spokesman for TWA, said.
Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport said it expects payment Friday from TWA for the $100,000 it owes.
"As of today, they are in arrears," Dallas/Fort Worth spokeswoman Angel Biasatti said, adding the airline has been sent notices. But she added that TWA has been "very cooperative."
Biasatti said this was the first time TWA was late in making its payments. If payment is received on Friday as promised, the airline's account will be current, she added.
TWA's Walker declined to comment on any of its airport payments. "Like any other company in the world, TWA has accounts payable," he said. "Our accounts payable do indeed get paid."
Wilson of San Francisco Airport said TWA has been an "excellent tenant," adding the airport has had "a wonderful working relationship with them."
"They are going through financial difficulties," Wilson said. "Being a public agency, the owner of the airport, we can't let them get by free for very long."

TWA said recently its first quarter operating loss will exceed the loss for the year-ago period. In a Securities and Exchange Commission filing, TWA also said its consolidated cash and cash equivalents balance at the end of 1996 was $181.6 million, down from $304.3 million on Dec. 31, 1995.
Its auditors, KPMG Peat Marwick LLP, said in an SEC filing that TWA's recurring losses and its limited sources of fresh cash raised substantial doubts about its future as a going concern.
Separately, TWA reached an agreement earlier this year with Logan International Airport in Boston to reduced its gates there to two from four.
Jeremy Crockford, a spokesman for the Massachusetts Port Authority, which operates Logan Airport, said the gates were reduced because of a lack of demand, not because of any financial reasons.
"It was mutually agreed to because of lack of use of the gates," Crockford said.
